goal: Keep the csv-report internal tool effective at turning the weekly CSV export into a summary report, while keeping it easy for the analyst to run and for the maintainer to evolve.
question: Should csv-report keep processing CSV with only the Python standard library, or add a third-party data-handling dependency for building the summary report?
known_constraints: The tool must run as a single script on the analyst's laptop (README.md).
Weekly input file sizes are unmeasured and vary a lot between weeks (README.md).
The repository currently has no dependency manifest or packaging layer (repository file listing).

environment.runtime_context: runs locally on the analyst's laptop, no server or deployment layer

evidence: README.md describes csv-report as 'An internal tool that turns the weekly CSV export into a summary report' (README.md).
The tool 'runs as a single script on the analyst's laptop'; there is no server, packaging, or deployment layer (README.md).
Data volume is unmeasured: 'Nobody has measured how large the weekly files get; sizes vary a lot between weeks' (README.md, verbatim quote).
process.py is currently standard-library only; its docstring says '(stdlib only today)' and the module imports only the csv module (process.py).
The only implemented summary operation is a row count: summarize(rows) returns sum(1 for _ in rows) over a lazily streamed csv.reader, so memory use is bounded today (process.py).
No dependency manifest exists in the repository: no pyproject.toml, requirements.txt, setup.py, setup.cfg, Pipfile, or lock files were found (repository file listing).
The local interpreter is Python 3.14.7 (python3 --version on this machine).

alternatives.name: Keep Standard Library Only
alternatives.description: Continue using Python's built-in csv module and implement any future summary logic as hand-written Python over streamed rows.
advantages: Zero dependencies: the single script runs on any machine with a Python interpreter, matching the analyst's-laptop constraint with no installation step.
csv.reader already streams row by row, so memory stays bounded even when weekly file sizes are unknown.
No versions to pin, audit, or upgrade, so there is no supply-chain or upgrade maintenance for an unowned internal tool.
disadvantages: Any real summary logic beyond a row count (grouping, aggregation, type conversion, date parsing) must be hand-written and tested by the maintainer.
Pure-Python row loops are the slowest of the three options if weekly files turn out to be very large.
Hand-rolled tabular transforms are a common source of subtle correctness bugs.
assumptions: The report needs only simple operations; the only implemented operation today is a row count.
Unmeasured file sizes stay within what a single pure-Python pass can process in acceptable time.

alternatives.name: Add pandas (DataFrame Library)
alternatives.description: Add pandas as a dependency and implement the summary report with DataFrame operations.
advantages: Provides well-tested primitives for grouping, aggregation, type inference, date parsing, and report-shaped output.
Very large user base and documentation, so future maintainers and analyst-oriented examples are easy to find.
Reduces hand-written parsing and aggregation code relative to the standard library.
disadvantages: Heavy install footprint (pandas plus numpy) on the analyst's laptop and requires introducing a dependency manifest the repository does not have.
The common read_csv path loads the whole file into memory, which is unbounded and unverified given that file sizes are unmeasured and vary a lot.
Version churn and upgrade maintenance for a single-script internal tool.
assumptions: The analyst's laptop can install and maintain third-party packages.
Future summaries need DataFrame-style grouping and aggregation enough to justify the added install weight.

alternatives.name: Add polars (Streaming DataFrame Library)
alternatives.description: Add polars as a dependency and implement the summary report with its lazy/streaming query engine.
advantages: Offers DataFrame-level aggregation primitives with a lazy engine designed to process data in bounded memory, which addresses the unmeasured file-size risk directly.
Columnar execution is fast on large tabular files, and the install footprint is smaller than pandas with numpy.
Reduces hand-written parsing and aggregation code relative to the standard library.
disadvantages: Still introduces a third-party dependency and a manifest to maintain for a currently dependency-free single script.
Smaller ecosystem and fewer analysts familiar with it compared with pandas.
Pre-1.0-style API churn in parts of its surface has historically required code updates across versions.
assumptions: Weekly files are large or the summary logic is complex enough that hand-written standard-library code becomes a real maintenance cost.
The analyst's environment can install compiled wheels.

criteria.name: Fit to current and foreseeable summary logic
rubric: Requires hand-built code for basic aggregation
Supports basic aggregation with modest hand-written glue
Provides broad aggregation, grouping, and type handling out of the box

criteria.name: Robustness to large and unmeasured file sizes
rubric: Loads the whole file into memory with no size safeguard
Streams row by row with bounded memory but pure-Python speed
Processes in bounded memory with a fast columnar or streaming engine

criteria.name: Ease of running and maintaining the single-script internal tool
rubric: Requires a new dependency manifest, environment setup, and ongoing upgrade maintenance
Adds a small amount of management overhead to the script
Runs on a bare Python installation with zero dependency management

criteria.name: Risk of subtle bugs in the summary output
rubric: All parsing and aggregation hand-written with no external test coverage
Mostly hand-written with limited library help
Parsing and aggregation handled by a widely tested library implementation

criteria.name: Throughput on large weekly files
rubric: Pure-Python row loop, slowest of the options
Accelerated execution, fast on large files
